video.title: Why Did Fallen Angels Marry Human Women?

transcript.text: For five chapters, Genesis has been counting Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan.
Each life is summed up in nearly the same words:
He lived, he had sons and daughters, and he died.
It is a slow drum beat, and every beat ends in the grave.
Then, in the sixth chapter, the drum beat breaks.
Two verbs take over.
They saw, they took.
No names are given, no reason is offered.
Within a few verses, God will say he regrets ever making humankind.
In between sit four short verses about the sons of God,
the daughters of men, and children who grew into the famous warriors of old.
Believers have argued over those verses for more than 2,000 years.
Who were these sons of God?
Why did they choose these women?
And why does a book that explains so much stay silent on the one question everyone asks?
Three answers have survived from the ancient world.
One of them leans on a book that a New Testament writer quotes by name.
Start with where the story sits.
Genesis 4 follows Cain's descendants, and it ends with a man named Lamech.
Lamech is the first person in scripture to take two wives.
He is also the first to boast about killing, composing a little song to his wives
about avenging himself 77fold.
Genesis 5 turns to the line of Seth, and the tone shifts.
There is a man named Enoch, who walked with God and then was simply gone, because God took him.
Hold on to that detail; it will matter later.
Then Genesis 6 opens.
Humanity is multiplying across the earth, and daughters are being born.
Verse 2 says that the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful,
and they took as wives whomever they chose.
Look closely at the grammar: they saw and they took,
and the text records no one else's choice in the matter.
The phrase "whomever they chose" reads like a hand reaching out and closing.
What follows is one of the most compressed passages in the Bible.
God declares that his spirit will not remain with humanity forever,
and he sets a limit of 120 years.
Many readers understand this as a countdown.
The text then mentions the Nephilim, who were on the earth in those days and also afterward.
They are called the mighty men of old, the men of renown.
Here is what the passage does not do.
It never says the union itself was a sin.
It never explains who the sons of God are.
It never says what the Nephilim were, beyond the fact that they existed.
The condemnation comes in the very next verse.
The Lord sees that human wickedness has grown great,
and that every inclination of the heart is only evil all the time.
The marriages sit right beside that verdict.
Genesis lets the reader draw the line between them.
So the first mystery is a matter of the text itself:
Why would a passage this important be written so quietly?
Everything hinges on two Hebrew words: Bene Ha Elohim, sons of God.
The oldest answer to who they were comes from the early church,
and by the fourth and fifth centuries it had become the dominant one.
Augustine championed it.
The sons of God were the godly line of Seth,
and the daughters of men were the women of Cain's line.
The tragedy in this reading was intermarriage.
Believers stopped being set apart and married for beauty alone,
and the whole human family drifted into wickedness.
This view has real strengths.
It stays entirely on the human level, and Genesis 4 and 5 do set up two family lines side by side.
But it also faces a question:
Genesis never calls Seth's descendants sons of God.
And if these were ordinary marriages between ordinary people, why does the text single out their children as mighty and famous?
A second view says the sons of God were ancient rulers,
kings who claimed divine status and took whatever women they pleased.
That fits the picture of men taken by force, and it echoes the kind of violence Lamech boasted about.
But the phrase itself is never used for kings in scripture.
The third view starts with the phrase itself.

transcript.text: In Job 1 and again in Job 2, the sons of God come to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan comes among them.
In Job 38, God asked Job where he was when the sons of God shouted for joy as the earth's foundations were laid.
In every one of those scenes, the sons of God are heavenly beings.
This is the detail many readers pass over.
If Genesis 6 uses the same phrase the same way, then these were not men at all.
This reading is also the oldest we can trace.
A number of early Jewish writers understood Genesis 6 this way, including the first century historian Josephus, who describes angels of God joining with women.
Many early Christian writers agreed, among them Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Tertullian.
These are traditions, and they should be weighed as traditions, not as scripture.
The angelic view has a serious objection to answer, and it comes from Jesus himself.
In Matthew 22, he says that in the resurrection, people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven.
If angels do not marry, how could these have taken wives?
Defenders of the angelic view reply that Jesus is speaking of angels in heaven in their proper place, and says nothing about beings who abandoned it.
Critics reply that this is an argument from silence.
The question stays honestly open.
Then there are two short New Testament letters that seem to know something Genesis never says.
Second Peter chapter 2 speaks of angels who sinned and were cast into chains of darkness, held for judgment.
Jude verse 6 speaks of angels who did not keep their proper dwelling and are now bound.
Neither letter mentions Genesis 6 by name.
Jude does, however, quote an ancient prophecy.
Word for word, he tells us whose words they were.
The quotation is from Enoch, the same Enoch who walked with God.
This is the part of the story Genesis never tells, though someone in the ancient world clearly did.
If you want to explore these ancient writings for yourself, click the link in this video's pinned comment to get the Book of Enoch, the complete collection of 1, 2, and 3.
A note on what this book is.
The story of the sons of God appears in the first of the Enoch writings, in the section called the Book of the Watchers.
Scholars generally date it to the 3rd century before Christ, and fragments in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church counts it as scripture.
Most other Christian traditions do not.
Jude quotes one line from it, but a quotation does not make an entire book canonical.
What follows is an ancient account, not the Bible's own.
According to that account, 200 angels called watchers looked down on the daughters of men.
The text says they saw them and desired them.
The Book of Enoch records their leader, Samjaza, hesitating.
He feared that he alone would pay for what they were about to do, so they bound themselves with an oath.
The text says they swore it on the summit of Mount Hermon, and it gives the mountain's name a meaning from that oath.
Then they descended and took wives.
The account does not stop at marriage.
The watchers taught the women charms, enchantments, and the cutting of roots.
One of them, Azazel, taught humanity to forge weapons and to craft ornaments and cosmetics.
The children born of these unions were giants who consumed the earth's food, then turned on humankind and finally on one another.
According to Enoch, the earth itself cried out, and the cry reached heaven.
Four archangels looked down from the sanctuary and saw blood spreading across the ground.
They brought the cry before God, and God sent them to bind the guilty watchers until the day of judgment.
Notice what has happened to the story.
Genesis gives us four verses and two verbs.
Enoch gives us an oath, a mountain, and a reason the earth became soaked in violence.
It is a rich account, and it was clearly known to the writers of Jude and 2nd Peter.
But it is not scripture, and Genesis itself never mentions teaching weapons or an oath.

transcript.text: What happens next is the part of the story that can be read in scripture itself.
In Second Peter, the sequence is clear.
The angels who sinned are cast down and held in chains.
In the very next verse, the ancient world is brought under the flood, and Noah is preserved.
The letter treats these as connected acts of judgment, though it does not spell out how.
Genesis agrees on the larger shape.
The Lord sees the wickedness, the earth is filled with violence, and then comes a sentence of deep sorrow.
The Lord regretted that he had made humankind, and it grieved him to his heart.
Pause on that.
The judgment of Genesis 6 is grief before it is anger.
Then comes the turn that makes the whole chapter breathe.
Verse 8 says, "But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord."
Set that beside everything we have read.
The sons of God saw and took.
Noah found.
One reaches out and grasps what is not his.
The other stands with open hands and receives what he never earned.
This is an observation about contrast in the text, but it carries the weight of the whole passage.
The story of Genesis 6 is about what happens when the creature takes what was never offered, and it is about the one who walked with God and was given away through the water.
So what can we say with confidence?
Scripture does not tell us who the sons of God were, only that the phrase appears in Job for heavenly beings.
It does not tell us what the Nephilim were.
It does not say why God permitted any of it.
What it shows is a world that reached beyond its limits, a creator who grieved, and a man who found favor.
Perhaps that is why the writer used only two verbs: they saw, they took.
Everything else grows out of that.
One question remains that Genesis leaves untouched.
Peter speaks of spirits in prison who disobeyed in the days of Noah, and scholars still debate who those spirits were and what Peter meant.
The ancient Enoch writings have their own answers, and reading them is the best way to see how early readers wrestled with it.
To explore more of these ancient writings, click the link in the pinned comment to get your copy of the Book of Enoch, the complete collection of 1, 2, and 3 Enoch Before the Flood.
Someone saw the world and took.
And before the flood, someone else stood quietly and was given grace.
Which of the three readings of the sons of God do you find most convincing, and why?
Tell me in the comments.
